The ferry left at six, and Marta was the only passenger who stayed on deck.

It was not a pleasant morning. The wind came across the harbour in short, cold pushes, and the gulls had given up on the sky and were standing in a row along the railing like commuters waiting for a late bus. She held her coffee with both hands and watched the town slide backwards: first the customs house, then the long green roof of the fish market, then the lighthouse that had not worked since before she was born.

"You'll freeze out here," said a voice behind her.

It belonged to the deckhand, a boy of perhaps nineteen with a yellow jacket two sizes too large. He was coiling a rope with the seriousness of someone who had recently been told off for coiling it badly.

"I like to see where I'm leaving," Marta said.

"Most people like to see where they're going." He nodded toward the bow, where the island was still only a darker line in the grey. "Forty minutes, if the engine behaves. It doesn't always."

"What happens when it doesn't?"

"We drift a bit. Old Tomas hits it with a spanner. Then it behaves." He grinned, pleased with the story, and she understood that he had told it many times and that it had never once failed him.

She had not been back to the island in eleven years. In her bag there was a set of keys she did not recognise, a letter from a lawyer written in the careful language that lawyers use when they are sorry, and a photograph of a house with blue shutters. Her aunt had left her the house. Nobody had asked whether she wanted it.

The engine coughed. The gulls, all together, turned their heads.

"There it goes," said the boy cheerfully, and from somewhere below came the unmistakable sound of metal striking metal, three times, with feeling. The engine thought about it, shuddered, and went on.

Marta laughed before she could stop herself. It was the first time she had laughed in a week, and it surprised her so much that she spilled the coffee on her sleeve.

"Told you," the boy said. He finished the rope, looked at it with open admiration, and then, because nobody was there to tell him otherwise, sat down on it. "Are you staying long?"

She looked at the island. It had grown while they talked. She could see the white mark of the chapel now, and below it the dark mouth of the little harbour, and she found that she remembered exactly how the water smelled there in summer, of tar and warm stone and oranges from the boat that came on Thursdays.

"I don't know yet," she said, which was the truth, and for once it did not feel like a problem.
